input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

Scientific fact-checking aims to determine the veracity of scientific claims by retrieving and analysing evidence from research literature. The problem is inherently more complex than general fact-checking since it must accommodate the evolving nature of scientific knowledge, the structural complexity of academic literature and the challenges posed by long-form, multimodal scientific expression. However, existing approaches focus on simplified versions of the problem based on small-scale datasets consisting of abstracts rather than full papers, thereby avoiding the distinct challenges associated with processing complete documents. This paper examines the limitations of current scientific fact-checking systems and reveals the many potential features and resources that could be exploited to advance their performance. The International Particle Physics Outreach Group (IPPOG) has been making concerted and systematic efforts to present and popularise particle physics across all audiences and age groups since 1997. Today the scientific community has in IPPOG a strategic pillar in fostering long-term, sustainable support for fundamental research around the world. One of the main tools IPPOG has been offering to the scientific community, teachers and educators for almost 10 years is the Resource Database (RDB), an online platform containing a collection of high quality engaging education and outreach materials in particle physics and related sciences.

[RID:web:paper:c3f69a669000] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2201.04672v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.04672v1" title="How Can Graph Neural Networks Help Document Retrieval: A Case Study on CORD19 with Concept Map Generation"
Graph neural networks (GNNs), as a group of powerful tools for representation learning on irregular data, have manifested superiority in various downstream tasks. With unstructured texts represented as concept maps, GNNs can be exploited for tasks like document retrieval. Intrigued by how can GNNs help document retrieval, we conduct an empirical study on a large-scale multi-discipline dataset CORD-19. Results show that instead of the complex structure-oriented GNNs such as GINs and GATs, our proposed semantics-oriented graph functions achieve better and more stable performance based on the BM25 retrieved candidates. Our insights in this case study can serve as a guideline for future work to develop effective GNNs with appropriate semantics-oriented inductive biases for textual reasoning tasks like document retrieval and classification. All code for this case study is available at https://github.com/HennyJie/GNN-DocRetrieval.

[RID:web:paper:f01cfad6741d] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2012.11740v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2012.11740v1" title="SChuBERT: Scholarly Document Chunks with BERT-encoding boost Citation Count Prediction"
Predicting the number of citations of scholarly documents is an upcoming task in scholarly document processing. Besides the intrinsic merit of this information, it also has a wider use as an imperfect proxy for quality which has the advantage of being cheaply available for large volumes of scholarly documents. Previous work has dealt with number of citations prediction with relatively small training data sets, or larger datasets but with short, incomplete input text. In this work we leverage the open access ACL Anthology collection in combination with the Semantic Scholar bibliometric database to create a large corpus of scholarly documents with associated citation information and we propose a new citation prediction model called SChuBERT. In our experiments we compare SChuBERT with several state-of-the-art citation prediction models and show that it outperforms previous methods by a large margin. We also show the merit of using more training data and longer input for number of citations prediction.
input.section_draft:
This work has presented a graph-guided prompting workflow for producing long-form scientific sections with an explicit emphasis on evidence and citation consistency. The method encodes section interdependencies in a document graph, enforces machine-checkable section outputs via a strict JSON schema, injects ranked evidence into section-level prompts, and assembles validated sections into a LaTeX manuscript with an accompanying refs.bib. The design choices prioritize auditability: every generated factual assertion is required to cite source material, and outputs are produced in a machine-readable form to simplify post hoc inspection and editing.

The paper contributes three practical artifacts intended to be useful beyond the immediate implementation: (1) a graph-based section scheduler that orders generation according to section dependencies (leaf-first writing), (2) an evidence-retrieval and injection protocol that scopes and anchors source material to individual sections, and (3) an audit-friendly JSON output format and assembly rules that integrate with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Together these components are intended to reduce unsupported assertions during generation and to make any remaining failures easier to detect and correct.

We evaluated the pipeline against a baseline linear prompting comparator using two topical domains and datasets composed of internal notes and a small curated PDF collection. Evaluation focused on citation coverage, unsupported-assertion rate, and reviewer-style quality scores; the full quantitative and qualitative results are reported in Section 5. Given the limited dataset scale and reliance on retrieval quality, the empirical findings are presented conservatively. The reported outcomes should therefore be interpreted as preliminary evidence that graph-aware sectioning can improve citation placement and reduce unsupported claims under the tested conditions, rather than definitive proof of broad generalization.

We explicitly document limitations and failure modes: dependence on the retrieval index and ranking, sensitivity to how section dependencies are encoded, and the constrained experimental scope (internal notes and a small curated PDF set). Practical mitigations include stronger retrieval re-ranking, human-in-the-loop verifications for high-stakes assertions, richer graph encodings to capture rhetorical relations, and staged validation checks during assembly.

For future work we advocate larger-scale and multi-domain evaluations, development of community-shared datasets and benchmark tasks that emphasize citation fidelity, and toolchains that make JSON-constrained section artifacts interoperable with common authoring workflows. Additional research directions include multi-stage retrieval strategies, automated detection and correction of unsupported claims, and user studies to quantify the human effort saved by machine-aided audits.

In closing, this paper advances a conservative, evidence-first approach to long-form scientific generation: by encoding document structure explicitly and requiring source-backed, machine-checked section outputs, we aim to make automatically generated drafts more reliable and more amenable to transparent human oversight.

This work has presented a graph-guided prompting workflow for producing long-form scientific sections with an explicit emphasis on evidence and citation consistency. The method encodes section interdependencies in a document graph, enforces machine-checkable section outputs via a strict JSON schema, injects ranked evidence into section-level prompts, and assembles validated sections into a LaTeX manuscript with an accompanying refs.bib. The design choices prioritize auditability: every generated factual assertion is required to cite source material, and outputs are produced in a machine-readable form to simplify post hoc inspection and editing.

The paper contributes three practical artifacts intended to be useful beyond the immediate implementation: (1) a graph-based section scheduler that orders generation according to section dependencies (leaf-first writing), (2) an evidence-retrieval and injection protocol that scopes and anchors source material to individual sections, and (3) an audit-friendly JSON output format and assembly rules that integrate with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Together these components are intended to reduce unsupported assertions during generation and to make any remaining failures easier to detect and correct. The use of graph structure to organize document elements and retrieval candidates is consonant with prior work that leverages graph encodings to improve document- and concept-level retrieval and representation \cite{2201.04672v1}.

We evaluated the pipeline against a baseline linear prompting comparator using two topical domains and datasets composed of internal notes and a small curated PDF collection. Evaluation focused on citation coverage, unsupported-assertion rate, and reviewer-style quality scores; the full quantitative and qualitative results are reported in Section 5. Given the limited dataset scale and reliance on retrieval quality, the empirical findings are presented conservatively. In particular, scientific fact-checking and evidence retrieval present complex challenges—including the need for structured document parsing, time-aware retrieval, and robust evidence ranking—which constrain broad generalization from small-scale experiments \cite{2506.20844v2}. The reported outcomes should therefore be interpreted as preliminary evidence that graph-aware sectioning can improve citation placement and reduce unsupported claims under the tested conditions, rather than definitive proof of wide applicability.

We explicitly document limitations and failure modes: dependence on the retrieval index and ranking, sensitivity to how section dependencies are encoded, and the constrained experimental scope (internal notes and a small curated PDF set). Practical mitigations include stronger retrieval re-ranking and multi-stage retrieval, human-in-the-loop verification for high-stakes assertions, richer graph encodings to capture rhetorical relations, and staged validation checks during assembly. Several of these mitigation directions reflect known needs for improved retrieval and document-chunk handling when processing long scholarly texts \cite{2506.20844v2,2012.11740v1}.

For future work we advocate larger-scale and multi-domain evaluations, development of community-shared datasets and benchmark tasks that emphasize citation fidelity, and toolchains that make JSON-constrained section artifacts interoperable with common authoring workflows. Additional research directions include multi-stage retrieval strategies, automated detection and correction of unsupported claims, and user studies to quantify the human effort saved by machine-aided audits. These directions are presented as proposals for further study rather than validated results.

In closing, this paper advances a conservative, evidence-first approach to long-form scientific generation: by encoding document structure explicitly and requiring source-backed, machine-checked section outputs, we aim to make automatically generated drafts more reliable and more amenable to transparent human oversight. This emphasis on explicit evidence injection and auditability responds to documented challenges in scientific fact-checking and structured-document retrieval, and it motivates continued empirical work on retrieval quality, graph encodings, and operational evaluation at scale \cite{2506.20844v2,2201.04672v1}.
